name: Mary's Room
statement: A scientist who knows every physical fact about colour but has only seen black and white still learns something new the day she first sees red.
statementAccent: still learns something new the day she first sees red
meaning: Mary's room, also called the knowledge argument, is a thought experiment proposed by the philosopher Frank Jackson in 1982 to challenge physicalism, the view that everything is physical. Mary is a brilliant scientist who has lived her whole life in a black-and-white room and learns about the world through a black-and-white monitor. She knows every physical fact there is about colour vision: the wavelengths of light, the workings of the retina and brain, the complete neuroscience. The question is what happens when Mary is finally released and sees a red object for the first time. If she learns something new, what it is like to see red, then there was a fact she did not know despite knowing all the physical facts, so not all facts are physical, and physicalism is false. Jackson later, notably, abandoned the argument and came to reject its conclusion.
mechanism: The argument has a simple structure. Premise one: before release, Mary knows all the physical facts about colour and colour vision. Premise two: on release, seeing red for the first time, she learns something new, namely what it is like to experience red, the qualitative feel philosophers call a quale. Conclusion: therefore there are non-physical facts, facts about conscious experience that no amount of physical knowledge captures, and physicalism is false. The target is the completeness of physical description: the claim that the felt quality of experience escapes even a total physical account. Physicalist replies deny one of the premises, arguing for instance that Mary gains not a new fact but a new ability or a new way of representing an old fact, the ability hypothesis, so that she learns how, not that. Jackson himself came to accept a reply of this kind and rejected the argument he had made famous.

examples.text: Mary, knowing all the physics and neuroscience of colour, leaves her black-and-white room and sees a red rose; the claim is that she now learns what red looks like.
Critics answer that Mary gains a new ability, to imagine and recognise red, rather than a new fact, so she learns how to do something, not a further truth.
Frank Jackson, who devised the argument, later changed his mind and came to reject its anti-physicalist conclusion, treating the intuition as misleading.

variants.name: The knowledge argument in general
variants.text: The broader family of arguments that conscious experience involves facts, or knowledge, that a complete physical description leaves out.

variants.name: The ability hypothesis
variants.text: The reply that on release Mary acquires practical abilities, to recognise and imagine colours, rather than knowledge of any new fact, so physicalism survives.

whyItMatters: Mary's room is one of the most discussed arguments in the philosophy of mind, a central challenge to physicalism and a focal point for debates about consciousness and qualia. It gives sharp form to the intuition that there is something about the felt quality of experience, what it is like to see red or feel pain, that seems to slip through any purely physical account, connecting to the wider hard problem of consciousness. The argument has generated a large literature of physicalist replies, the ability hypothesis, the old-fact-new-guise response, and others, making it a testing ground for theories of mind. Its afterlife is unusually pointed because its own author later rejected it, which itself became part of the debate over whether the intuition it trades on can be trusted.

weigh whether what she gains is really a new fact, or instead a new ability or a new way of grasping a fact she already knew.

limits: The knowledge argument turns on the contested premise that Mary learns a new fact rather than a new ability or a new mode of presentation of an old fact, so its conclusion is not settled but one side of an active debate. Physicalists offer several replies, the ability hypothesis and the old-fact-new-guise response among them, each denying that anything non-physical need be involved. Strikingly, Frank Jackson, who framed the argument, later abandoned it and rejected its dualist upshot, holding that the intuition misleads. The experiment therefore establishes an intuition to be explained rather than a proven metaphysical result, and how much weight it can bear depends on unresolved questions about the nature of knowledge and consciousness.
misreadings: The argument does not prove dualism outright; it presents an intuition, that Mary learns something new, that physicalists dispute by denying she gains a genuine new fact. What Mary lacks in the room is not physical information but, on the leading physicalist reply, certain abilities or first-person acquaintance, so learning may be a matter of how, not that. And the case is not endorsed by consensus or even by its author's final view: Jackson himself came to reject the conclusion, so citing Mary's room as settling the matter against physicalism misrepresents its standing.
origin: Devised by the philosopher Frank Jackson in his 1982 paper Epiphenomenal Qualia, and elaborated in What Mary Didn't Know in 1986, as an argument against physicalism; Jackson later abandoned the argument and rejected its conclusion.
